title: GARLIC: Graph Attention for Irregular ICU Time Series
one_liner: GARLIC predicts patient outcomes from messy hospital sensor readings by learning which sensors matter most and how they interact, all visible inside the model.
lead: Hospitals collect dozens of measurements from each patient—heart rate, oxygen, blood pressure—but the readings arrive at random times and many go missing. A doctor needs both a good prediction of what will happen (mortality, infection risk) and a clear explanation of why. GARLIC does both: it fills in the missing measurements, learns which sensors matter for the prediction, and shows you exactly which values triggered the alarm.

problem.h2: Why hospital sensor data is hard
paras: Hospital ICUs (Intensive Care Units) record dozens of sensors every minute—heart rate, oxygen levels, blood pressure, lab test results. But the readings don't arrive on a regular schedule. A blood test might happen every 8 hours; heart rate is recorded every second. Many values go missing. A doctor faces a puzzle: given all this chaotic, incomplete data, will this patient get worse in the next week? And when the model says yes, why did it say that?

Doctors need both accuracy and explanation. A black-box predictor that just outputs a number is not useful in the ICU—a clinician has to trust the reasoning. Old methods either are accurate but opaque, or interpretable but miss patterns. No method has done both well while handling the messy timing and missing values.

callout.html: Learn to predict patient outcomes from irregular, incomplete sensor time series while showing doctors exactly which measurements and which sensors mattered for each prediction.

steps.text: Read all sensor values, tag what is observed vs missing.
Estimate missing values using recent history; older history counts less.
For recent history, learn which sensors correlate, store as edges.
Pass sensor values along graph edges; each sensor absorbs its neighbors' info.
At each time step, learn a weight for each sensor; sum weighted signals.
Learn which time steps matter; average the signal-weighted values over time.
Output risk score; return learned importance weights and graph as explanations.

paras: The paper learns three things jointly: (1) how to fill in missing sensor values, (2) the graph of which sensors depend on each other, and (3) the weights that say which sensor is important at which time.
object.object: learned importance weights and sensor graph

hidden.h2: Signal importance: which sensor matters now
hidden.name: Signal importance weight
paras: At any given moment, not all sensors are equally important for predicting the outcome. The paper learns an importance weight for each sensor at each time step. A weight of 0 means ignore this sensor; a weight of 1 means trust it fully. These weights are the model's way of saying which signals were the key drivers of the prediction.

The paper estimates these weights by learning attention: a small neural network that takes the sensor reading and outputs a number between 0 and 1. Unlike typical machine learning models where importance is hidden, these weights are baked into the model's structure and come out directly as explanations.

heat.caption: Darker means the model pays more attention. Borders mark the top critical signals.

reads.html: The model trains by seeing thousands of patients and learning: when these sensors spike together, bad outcomes follow; ignore the others.

The paper compresses learned attention matrices and sparsifies the sensor graph by adding a penalty term that pushes weak connections toward zero, yielding concise importance scores for each sensor and edge.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: three pieces talking
paras: Standard neural networks are black boxes. GARLIC trades some flexibility for transparency by building explanation directly into the architecture.

The trick is structure. Instead of a dense black-box network, GARLIC has three layers of explicit design: (1) when a value is missing, predict it from recent history (exponential decay), so the input is always complete. (2) Build a sensor-to-sensor connection graph by looking at temporal correlations; update the graph end-to-end as the model trains. (3) At each time step, apply attention: score each sensor (the learned weights), then score each time step. The output of each attention layer is a set of numbers (the weights themselves), which are your explanation.

The magic is that attention weights serve double duty: they compute the prediction (weighted sum of inputs), and they are also the explanation (which inputs were used). No external explanation method needed. As the model trains to predict outcomes, it automatically learns which sensors to trust.

stages.s: Graph message passing: sensors share info
Temporal attention: score each time step
Risk score plus learned attention weights as explanation

math.words: The prediction is a sum of signal contributions, where each signal is weighted by its learned importance, and the importance comes from applying a learned attention function to the sensor reading. The final output sums over time steps, weighting recent and urgent time steps more.
math.equation: output = sum_t { alpha_time(t) * sum_k { alpha_signal(k, t) * embedding(k, t) } }
symbols: attention weight for sensor k at time step t (ranges from 0 to 1)
attention weight for time step t (ranges from 0 to 1)
the imputed or observed value of sensor k at time step t, after passing through the graph
the predicted risk score (0 to 1, where 1 means high risk of bad outcome)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have 3 sensors (heart rate, oxygen, blood pressure) at 2 time steps.
Time step 1: heart_rate=92, oxygen=98, pressure=120. Learned weights: 0.8, 0.1, 0.3. Weighted sum = 0.8*92 + 0.1*98 + 0.3*120 = 73.6 + 9.8 + 36 = 119.4.
Time step 2: heart_rate=105, oxygen=95, pressure=115. Learned weights: 0.9, 0.05, 0.2. Weighted sum = 0.9*105 + 0.05*95 + 0.2*115 = 94.5 + 4.75 + 23 = 122.25.
Temporal weights: time 1 gets 0.3, time 2 gets 0.7 (recent moments weighted more). Final output = 0.3*119.4 + 0.7*122.25 = 35.82 + 85.58 = 121.4. Normalized to a 0-1 risk: approximately 0.78 risk.

math.note: The model learns all these weights end-to-end from patient data, so the attention numbers capture real clinical patterns in which sensors predict death or infection.

bars.h2: What GARLIC gains over naive baselines

charts.title: Naive approach (ignore timing, drop missing values)
charts.note: Most models either drop incomplete records (lose data) or assume all sensors matter equally (miss the real patterns).

charts.title: GARLIC (learned attention + graph)
charts.note: GARLIC fills missing data, learns sensor importance, and keeps records intact. Doctors get both a strong prediction and a transparent reason.

items.html: If the training data has a spurious correlation (two sensors that happen to correlate by coincidence), the model will learn a fake edge in the sensor graph. A spurious edge can pull the model toward the wrong sensor at test time.
On a small dataset, the model may learn to weight one sensor extremely high (weight 0.99, others near 0) to fit the training patients, then fail on new patients where that sensor is less predictive.

If a patient's condition changes suddenly (a sensor suddenly drops), the exponential decay will still guess a smooth value. For a time step with missing blood pressure right after a sudden bleed, the imputed value may be dangerously optimistic.

Use L1 regularization to keep the attention weights from getting too extreme (force some signals to have small weight). Use feature-removal trials to verify that high-weight sensors truly predict outcomes. Validate on held-out patients from different hospitals.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a standard ICU dataset (MIMIC-III or PhysioNet). Train GARLIC and a naive baseline on 80 percent of the patients. On the remaining 20 percent, compute: (1) prediction accuracy (how many mortality predictions were correct), (2) remove the top 50 percent of high-importance sensors and run the model on new patient data, check that accuracy drops; remove a random 50 percent, check that it barely drops. This proves the model really learned which sensors matter. (3) For a few individual patients where the model predicted high risk, show the patient's sensor time series with importance weights painted on—confirm that high-weight sensors match the clinical events (e.g., high weight on heart rate during tachycardia, high weight on respiratory rate during respiratory failure).
demo.metric_eq: Feature importance fidelity = accuracy_full - accuracy_top50_removed (large drop) minus accuracy_random50_removed (small drop).
demo.closing: The demo must show that removing high-attention sensors hurts predictions, removing random sensors barely hurts, and attention weights align with real clinical deterioration events.
